title: A million labels, and which are wrong
teaches: A labelling platform: the label record, guidelines and their versions, overlap and agreement, gold questions and audits, model pre-labels, and active learning

parts.title: An answer key with mistakes in it

blocks.text: Every result in lesson P1 depends on labels. Someone has to mark which boxes contain pedestrians before an evaluation pipeline can count how many the model detected. In March 2021 Curtis Northcutt, Anish Athalye and Jonas Mueller, of MIT and Amazon Web Services, published a study of the labels in the test sets of ten widely used machine-learning benchmarks, including ImageNet, CIFAR-10, MNIST and QuickDraw. They used a statistical method called confident learning, which flags examples where the given label disagrees with a trained model's high-confidence prediction. They then recruited five Amazon Mechanical Turk reviewers per example to verify each flagged item.[^cl]

On average at least 3.3% of the test labels across the ten sets were wrong. ImageNet's validation set, the set on which a decade of image models had been ranked, held 2,916 errors, about 6% of its 50,000 images. QuickDraw's test set was about 10% wrong. The errors also changed conclusions. When the authors built test sets in which mislabelled examples made up a larger share, a smaller image model ranked above a larger one, whose lead had partly come from matching the wrong labels. The original test sets did not show the reversal, but they showed how close it was.[^flip]

In this lesson, we will design the **labelling platform** that produces the fleet's labels: the boxes drawn around objects in camera frames and the tags attached to short clips ("cyclist overtaking", "roadworks"). It must produce about a million labels a month for several teams, with a workforce of a few hundred labellers and a model that suggests labels, and it must be able to say, with evidence, how many of those labels are wrong.

parts.title: What it must do, and what it need not

blocks.text: **Functional.** The platform must accept labelling requests from teams, each with its items, its labelling guideline and its deadline; route each task to labellers qualified for that kind of work; collect labels, settle disagreements and publish finished labels to the datasets of lesson P3; measure and report quality for every task type and every labeller; choose which unlabelled items are most worth labelling next; and remove faces and number plates from images before any labeller sees them.

**Non-functional.** The platform must deliver a million labels a month at a known cost, with an error rate each team can rely on and that the platform can measure rather than assume. Every label must be traceable to the person or model that produced it and to the guideline version they followed.
**Out of scope.** We will not design the drawing tools in the labelling interface, or the hiring, training and payment of the workforce.

A million labels a month is about 33,000 a day. Our items are a frame with a few boxes or one clip tag, which take a trained labeller about a minute each, and three hundred labellers working seven-hour days give about 126,000 minutes a day, so each of the 33,000 items can get about four minutes of attention in total, but not much more. That budget governs the platform's design, because every quality check consumes labeller-minutes that cannot be spent producing new labels.

One labeller per item costs 1 minute per label and leaves every individual mistake in place. Two labellers per item, with an expert settling cases where they disagree, costs a little over 2 minutes per label and catches most individual slips. Letting the model's own label through without human review whenever the model is very confident costs no labeller time for those items, though it requires the calibration checks described below, and its errors enter the training data unseen.

A **label** is an answer attached to an item by a person or a model, such as a box with a class or a tag on a clip. Every label is made under a **labelling guideline**, the document that specifies what counts: whether a person pushing a bicycle is a pedestrian or a cyclist, whether a parked car's open door is part of the car, and how small an object must be to be left unlabelled. Guidelines change often as teams encounter cases the guideline did not foresee. A guideline change is a common cause of a bad batch, where half the labels follow the old reading and half follow the new one.

The platform's central data structure follows from that requirement. Each label is an immutable **label event**: the item identifier and its version, who or what produced it, the guideline version, the model suggestion shown at the time if any, the time spent in seconds, and a timestamp. Events are strictly append-only. The **current label** of an item is a view computed from its events by a deterministic rule: the latest reclassification under the current guideline takes priority, followed by the expert's ruling, and finally the agreed answer. A guideline change is recorded as new events, and the view is then recomputed.

blocks.caption: One item's label events. Two labellers disagreed, an expert settled it, and a guideline change later reclassified it; the current label is derived from all four.

blocks.text: Keeping an append-only log of events instead of overwriting a label in place requires extra storage, but it provides three operational benefits. Engineers can trace a label to its source when someone questions it. A guideline change can be applied to old labels by appending events, without discarding what labellers originally submitted. Finally, the quality measurements in the next section require the individual answers rather than just the final consensus.
Nobody can check every label, so the platform measures quality by sampling. Three mechanisms are standard, and they measure different failure modes.

**Overlap** sends the same item to two or three labellers independently. **Agreement** is how often their answers match. For tags it is a share of items; for boxes, two boxes match when they overlap enough, usually when the area they share is at least half the area they cover together (an **intersection over union** of 0.5). Disagreements go to an expert, or the majority answer wins with three labellers; a better combination weights each labeller by a statistical estimate of how reliable they are, the Dawid and Skene model.[^ds]

**Gold questions** are items whose right answer is already known, mixed into each labeller's queue without markers, so that the platform measures each labeller's accuracy continuously. Gold items must look like ordinary work, be drawn from hard cases as well as easy ones, and be rotated regularly so labellers do not memorise them.
An **audit** has an expert re-label a random sample of finished labels, a few per cent of each batch, and gives the platform its best estimate of the true error rate.

Agreement is not the same as correctness. Overlap catches individual slips, the errors one labeller makes and another does not. It cannot catch errors that labellers share. When a guideline is unclear on some kind of item, labellers who read it the same way agree on the same wrong answer, and majority voting makes the wrong answer look more certain. A model's suggestions introduce another source of shared errors, as two labellers who both accept the same nearly right suggestion agree on its mistake. Gold questions miss these errors as well, because they are usually written from cases whose answer is clear. Only an audit of a random sample, by someone who knows what the guideline means, measures them. In the workbench below, find a setting the platform can afford in which the labels are at most 3% wrong, measured by a random audit.

blocks.caption: A labelling line for 1,000 items. The bars compare the error the team measures with the true error, split by where it comes from. Rates are round figures of our own.
blocks.task: Get the true error to 3% or less, at 33,000 labels a day or more, measured by a random audit

blocks.text: No amount of overlap fixes an unclear guideline; the fix is to rewrite the guideline, which is why the platform tracks audit errors by guideline section, along with the disputes labellers raise, and sends the sections with the most errors back to the team that owns the guideline. Overlap is worth paying for on hard task types and for new labellers. The platform can also adjust overlap per labeller: a labeller whose gold accuracy is high gets single-labelled work, whereas one whose accuracy drops receives more overlap and fewer tasks.

A model trained on earlier labels can do part of the work. In **model-assisted labelling**, it draws its own boxes first and the labeller corrects them, which can be much faster than drawing from nothing. This introduces an operational risk: people tend to accept a suggestion that is nearly right. This cognitive bias, known as **anchoring**, allows a model's systematic mistakes to survive review more often than if the labeller started from a blank frame. The platform measures anchoring by seeding a few gold items with deliberately wrong suggestions and counting how often labellers accept them without change.

The model can also label some items with no human review when its confidence is above a threshold. That automation is safe only if the confidence is **calibrated**[^calibration]: among items labelled with 95% confidence, about 95% should be right, and that must hold for each class and slice separately, since a model can be well calibrated overall and confidently wrong on a rare class. Calibration has to be checked for each new model version, on a random sample with audited labels, because a model's confidence scores shift when it is retrained. Labels accepted this way also feed back into training. If they are wrong, the next model learns the same mistakes with more confidence, and the next round accepts more of them. The workbench shows the share of errors that come from labels nobody looked at.

The model can also choose what to label. **Active learning** sends people the items the model is least certain about, or the items least like anything in the training data, instead of a random sample. For a fleet that records far more than anyone can label, this concentrates the labelling budget on the cases that teach the model most; the onboard triggers of lesson D5 are a first stage of the same idea. Active learning has one important side effect: the items it chooses are deliberately unusual, so error rates and model accuracy measured on them say nothing about ordinary driving. The platform therefore always keeps a separate stream of randomly chosen items, labelled with the same care, for audits and for the evaluation sets of lesson P1. Labels for evaluation and golden sets, including the disagreements that shadow mode sends here in lesson P1, start from a blank frame, never from a suggestion made by a model under comparison, because anchoring would pull the right answers towards that model and flatter it in lesson P1.

The platform is a queue of tasks with many producers and many consumers, built on the same parts as the job scheduler of lesson D6. Each task carries a type (boxes on a frame, tags on a clip), the guideline version, a priority and a deadline. Labellers hold **qualifications** per task type, earned on a test set and kept up by their gold accuracy, and pull tasks they are qualified for. A labeller claims a task with a **lease**, a claim that expires unless renewed, as the workers in lesson D6 do, so a task abandoned by a labeller who walks away returns to the queue. Teams share the workforce through quotas, and a team with a release deadline can raise the priority of its tasks within its quota.

Before any image reaches the queue, a separate service detects faces and number plates and blurs them, because labellers often work for an outside vendor and see thousands of images of public streets a day. The platform records which version of the blurring model processed each image, as it records everything else. The blurred copy is for labellers only. Training reads the original images under access control. A team that trains on blurred images instead must also blur what the vehicle's model sees in deployment; otherwise, a model trained on blurred faces and run on unblurred cameras would suffer from training-serving skew (lesson P5).

Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth, launched in 2018, offers most of this design as a service. It sends each item to several labellers and combines their answers with a statistical model of each labeller's reliability rather than an unweighted vote. Its automated labelling retrains a model iteratively as labels arrive, labels items itself where the model is confident, and sends the rest to people. Commercial labelling companies sell the same pieces: overlap, gold questions, review queues and model pre-labels.

The confident learning method that found the benchmark errors is published as an open-source library, cleanlab. It works after the fact: given labels and a model's predicted probabilities, it ranks the labels most likely to be wrong, so experts can review those first. Teams use it beside random audits, not instead of them, because it finds the errors a model notices and can miss the ones a model shares.

parts.title: At ten and a hundred times

blocks.text: **At ten times** (ten million labels a month), the workforce grows to thousands across several vendors, and quality must be measured per vendor and per site as well as per labeller. Guidelines multiply with task types, and each one has an owner, a version history and a changelog that labellers see. Labeller drift, a slow change in how a whole group reads a guideline, shows up as a trend in gold accuracy and in audit results, and the platform alerts on it as with service error-rate alerts against service-level objectives (SLOs) in lesson 24.

**At a hundred times**, people cannot label most of what the fleet records. Most labels are proposed by models, and people check samples, settle disputes and label the cases models handle worst. The design's centre of gravity moves from the labelling queue to the measurements: random audits, calibration checks for every model version that is allowed to label, and the separate random stream that keeps evaluation honest. The label event store becomes one of the largest datasets the organisation keeps, and is managed like the versioned datasets of lesson P3.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on producing labels you can trust
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Two labellers label every item from a blank frame, with no model suggestions shown, and they agree on 98% of them. An expert audit of a random sample finds 6% of final labels wrong. What best explains the gap?
choices: The audit sample was too small to measure anything, so its 6% should be ignored in favour of agreement
The labellers are copying each other's answers, so they should be moved to separate teams
The labellers share a wrong reading of an unclear part of the guideline, so they agree on the same wrong answer
items.why: Overlap catches slips that one labeller makes and the other does not. Errors from an ambiguous guideline are shared, so labellers agree on them; only a random audit by someone who knows the intended answer measures them.

items.ask: A team lets its model label any item it is at least 95% confident about, with no person involved. What must it check before trusting those labels?
choices: That the model is at least as accurate as the labellers on the gold questions
That about 95% of items labelled at 95% are right, for each class and slice, checked by audit for each version
That the model's average confidence on an audited sample is at least 95%
items.why: A confidence threshold means something only if the model is calibrated, and calibration shifts with every retraining. Wrong labels accepted unseen feed the next training round, so the check is repeated per version.

items.ask: Labellers correct the model's suggested boxes instead of drawing from nothing, and throughput doubles. What should the platform add to measure the hidden cost?
choices: Gold items with deliberately wrong suggestions, counting how often they are accepted
More gold questions drawn from easy, clear cases
A check that every labeller changes at least one box per frame
items.why: People tend to accept suggestions that are nearly right, which lets the model's systematic mistakes through. Seeding known-wrong suggestions measures that anchoring directly.

items.ask: Active learning sends labellers only the frames the model is least sure about. Six months later, a team proposes building next quarter's evaluation set from those labelled frames. What is the problem?
choices: Frames chosen by a model can't be labelled as accurately as random frames
The frames were labelled by more experienced labellers, so they are too clean
Those frames are deliberately unusual, so scores on them don't describe ordinary driving; evaluation needs a random stream
items.why: Active learning biases the labelled set towards hard cases on purpose. Error rates and model scores measured on it mean nothing for real driving, so a separate random stream is kept for audits and evaluation.

items.ask: A guideline changes so that a person pushing a bicycle becomes "pedestrian with bicycle" instead of "cyclist". What does a store of append-only label events allow that overwriting labels in place does not?
choices: Storing the new labels in less space, since only the change needs to be kept
Re-deriving every affected item's current label under the new guideline while keeping what labellers originally said
Making the change take effect instantly on models already trained on the old labels
items.why: With events, the current label is a view computed by a rule. A guideline change adds events or changes the rule, and the history remains for tracing and for measuring labellers.

items.ask: A labelling platform has a budget of about four labeller-minutes per item. Which way of spending it buys the most trustworthy error figure?
choices: Two labellers with expert adjudication, plus a 2% random expert audit
Three labellers on every item, with a majority vote
One labeller per item, with the minutes saved spent on more gold questions
items.why: Overlap reduces slips, and the random audit measures what overlap cannot see. A third labeller adds cost but no measurement of shared errors; gold questions measure labellers on known cases, not the batch.

items.ask: Why must gold questions look like ordinary work and be rotated?
choices: So that the gold set keeps up with the newest sections of the guideline
So labellers can't recognise them and take more care on them than on ordinary items
So that gold accuracy can be compared fairly across labellers on different task types
items.why: If labellers can tell which items are gold, their gold accuracy measures their best behaviour rather than their usual work.

summary: **Test sets have wrong answers too.** Even standard benchmarks hold enough wrong labels to change which model ranks first.
**Keep labels as an append-only record.** Each label event records its source, guideline version and the suggestion shown; the current label is a view derived from the events.
**Guideline changes cause bad batches.** Version the guideline with every label, and send the sections with most disputes back to their owners.
**Agreement is not correctness.** Overlap catches individual slips; labellers who share a wrong reading agree on it, and only an expert audit of a random sample measures that.
**Gold questions measure labellers, not batches.** They must look like ordinary work and be rotated, and they usually miss the ambiguous cases.
**A model in the loop needs its own checks.** Measure anchoring with deliberately wrong suggestions, and accept unseen model labels only from a calibrated model, checked for each version.
**Active learning spends the budget well and biases the sample.** Keep a random stream for audits and evaluation.
**Labelling is a queue with leases and quotas.** Route tasks by qualification and priority, and blur faces and plates before anyone sees the images.

cl.title: Confident learning
cl.text: The method, published by Northcutt, Lu Jiang and Isaac Chuang in 2021, estimates for each pair of classes how often an example labelled as one is really the other, from a model's predicted probabilities on examples it did not train on. Examples whose label the model contradicts with high confidence are flagged as likely errors. The benchmark study then had people check every flagged example; an example was counted as an error only when a majority of five reviewers agreed.

flip.title: A conditional result
flip.text: The ranking change did not appear on the original test sets. The authors removed correctly labelled examples to raise the share of mislabelled ones, measured accuracy against the corrected labels, and found that ResNet-18 overtook ResNet-50 once the share of originally mislabelled examples rose by about 6 percentage points. The study was presented at NeurIPS 2021, and its corrected labels are published at labelerrors.com.

ds.title: Doctors who disagree
ds.text: The usual statistical model for combining labellers comes from medicine. In 1979 A. P. Dawid and A. M. Skene estimated how often each of several doctors misjudged patients' fitness for anaesthesia, with no true answers to compare against, by fitting each doctor's tendency to confuse one category with another from the patterns of disagreement alone. The same model weights a reliable labeller's answer more heavily than an unreliable one's.

calibration.title: Measuring calibration
calibration.text: A model is well calibrated when its predicted probability matches empirical frequency: among predictions assigned a confidence score of 0.90, exactly 90% should be correct. Machine-learning pipelines quantify this using Expected Calibration Error (ECE), which partitions predictions into confidence bins, computes the absolute difference between accuracy and confidence in each bin, and takes a weighted average across all bins. When neural networks become overconfident, engineers restore calibration using techniques such as temperature scaling on a held-out validation dataset.
